Physics, objects & tools across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Between five and seven, physics and object understanding shifts from single-rule heuristics to integrating mass, support, and motion, producing a paradox: rich implicit know-how alongside systematic explicit errors. Early on, many still show pre-operational biases (appearance-based judgments, animistic force reasoning); by six to seven, concrete-operational logic emerges: conservation of number and mass, multi-factor causal reasoning, and impersonal physical rules (unsupported objects fall, solids don’t interpenetrate). This is not a threshold but a long tuning phase: everyday manipulation, construction, and sport supply dense error signals that refine context-bound heuristics into nascent, rule-governed reasoning. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

By age six, children reason above chance when multiple forces act along a single dimension, marking the first reliable step beyond the single-force regime documented at four to five years, yet most elementary-school children still consider either the direction or the magnitude of both force vectors but not both simultaneously, with their preferred strategy varying by problem context 1. When two force vectors are not parallel, five- and six-year-olds focus on a single dominant cause 2, and predictions remain significantly less accurate when forces are placed on two dimensions, with perpendicular "Prevent" relations (where one force opposes or deflects another at ninety degrees) proving especially difficult compared to simpler "Cause" or "Enable" configurations 3, 4. The developmental progression moves from understanding a single force toward grasping enabling forces and ultimately preventative relations 2, but throughout the five-to-seven window, children’s physics engine remains functionally single-threaded for non-aligned forces: they serially process the most salient influence rather than computing a true vector sum, only beginning to compose forces into net effects when those forces are collinear, equally weighted, and presented in low-complexity contexts. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Five- to seven-year-olds increasingly bind appearance and dynamics to hidden material properties. They read weight from others’ actions (e.g., lift kinematics) 5, though judgments still lag adults’ accuracy, and their own anticipatory grip/load control shows shorter-latency, more adult-like scaling to expected weight and surface resistance 6, supporting gentler handling of "fragile" vs. "sturdy" objects in practice. For flexibility/softness, children begin to exploit deformation and optical cues, yet material perception remains single-cue biased: optimal visuo-haptic combination for texture/softness and shape-from-touch typically does not mature until  8-10, so 5-7-year-olds’ judgments can shift with the sensing modality 7, 8. Relatedly, school-age material categorization from images relies more on local/textural features (instead of global features) and only gradually becomes adult-like over later childhood 9, reflecting immature material-to-object-class mappings. Based on naturalistic observations, however, by age seven children do possess an extensive, largely implicit database of object-property associations accumulated through years of manipulation and observation (e.g knowing that ceramic mugs shatter when dropped, blankets are soft and flexible, rubber balls bounce, paper tears easily, and metal is hard) though this knowledge remains action-grounded and context-dependent rather than organized into explicit material-science categories; for example, 5-7-year-olds have been documented as having the core of their "weight" concept being felt/experienced weight and as having material kinds defined in terms of properties of large scale objects (as opposed to objects’ constituent parts) 10. Essentially, their everyday "material intuition" guides force selection, grip configuration, and risk assessment during handling, effectively functioning as a look-up table indexed by object identity rather than a compositional model that predicts novel material behaviors from first principles. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Conservation understanding (recognizing that quantity remains invariant despite perceptual transformation) follows a hierarchical acquisition sequence, with number conservation typically mastered around age six 11, 12, followed by mass and length around age seven, weight around age nine, and volume not until roughly age ten 13. Mechanistically, success at this age reflects two linked advances: children can mentally reverse the change (reversibility/compensation) and they can inhibit the misleading "longer = more" heuristic; neuroimaging of number-conservation shows parietal circuits for reversibility (intraparietal sulcus) coupled with right inferior frontal engagement for inhibitory control 14, 15, 16. This new control generalizes: brief embodied participation in the transformation (pouring/spreading it themselves) boosts 6-7-year-olds’ conservation 17, suggesting that dense action-coupled error continues to be the primary teaching signal even as explicit logical reasoning begins to emerge.

Kinematic prediction continues its dual-track development: implicit, cerebellum-mediated anticipatory control improves steadily (supporting cleaner catches, better batting timing, and smoother interceptive actions across childhood), yet explicit trajectory reasoning remains error-prone and context-dependent. In occluded-target pursuit, 5-7-year-olds already generate anticipatory saccades and sustain predictive smooth eye movements qualitatively like adults (albeit lower gain, higher error) 18. Sensitivity to inertia emerges around 5-6 years in predictive-judgment tasks 19, and while explicit projectile-motion predictions remain vulnerable to salient context 20, children’s estimates become more constraint-consistent than a year earlier, aligning their explicit judgments with the improving implicit controllers described for the 4- to 5-year window. The same calibration shows up in perception-action coupling: judgments of "can I fit/reach through this opening?" become much more adult-like by  7, with fewer unsafe attempts and tighter action scaling to aperture size 21, evidence that affordance perception is being recast in body- and task-scaled coordinates rather than visual salience alone.

Tool use and understanding in the 5-7 window shifts from reactive grip selection toward prospective, efficiency-driven planning, though tool innovation remains severely limited. By  7 many children now plan grasps for end-state comfort reliably when tasks impose competing demands (e.g., orientation + precision/force), a capacity that is weak or inconsistent at 5 and that first emerges under multi-constraint loads around 7 22, 23. Four- to five-year-olds exhibit high intra-individual variability (Siegler’s "overlapping waves"), simultaneously deploying infantile, transitional, and adult-like strategies within single sessions, whereas seven-year-olds consolidate toward the efficient solution and rarely revert 23, suggesting that five-to-seven marks the period when sensitivity to implementation costs drives competitive displacement of immature strategies. Yet important limits remain at 7: spontaneous tool innovation (e.g., bending a pipe-cleaner into a hook, or coordinating two tools concurrently) is still rare despite competent tool use and learning from demonstration, underscoring that abstract means-end synthesis lags behind improved affordance calibration 24, 25, 26. Seven-year-olds thus possess reliable prospective planning for known tool-object pairings and efficient grip implementation but lack the flexible reshaping and mechanical problem-solving that characterizes later childhood tool cognition.

The capabilities emerging during this stage point to a broader representational shift: by six to seven, children are learning that objects possess abstract, invariant properties (volume, mass, material kind) that persist across perceptual changes, but they still frequently default to appearance- and experience-based heuristics when task demands are high or contextual cues mislead, revealing that these emerging concepts are probabilistic priors being tuned by dense naturalistic error rather than crisp, rule-governed modules; their intuitive physics is transitioning from purely perceptual-motor prediction toward nascent explicit, depersonalized reasoning, but the explicit layer remains shallow, domain-specific, and easily overridden by salient perceptual features, a learning regime where everyday manipulation, construction play, and sports continue to generate the dense, action-coupled error streams that will eventually compile fragile heuristics into robust, generalizable physical models. We can say, however, that by about age six, most children maintain an implicit, globally consistent 3D scene representation with object individuation, coarse (and unreliable) material/affordance labels, and simple physical dynamics sufficient for planning and re-planning, while adult-like metric precision, cue-combination, and multi-object dynamics mature later (likely from  7-12). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).
